newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-European shares sharply down on rate worries.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-European shares sharply down on rate worries.

text.p: European bourses slipped sharply in early trading on Thursday, weighed down by another fall on Wall Street and concerns about interest rates on both sides of the Atlantic.
The dollar also edged lower from early levels against the mark and yen in thin early business, subdued by a holiday in Japan and caution ahead of key events later in the day.
The initial market focus was on a rate-setting meeting of Germany's Bundesbank, but analysts did not expect any change to the central bank's credit policy.

"We don't expect the Bundesbank to do anything today," said Roger Francis, senior analyst at IBJ International in London. "Two to three months ago a lot of people were anticipating a cut in German rates, but now that view has completely reversed."

Another focus was U.S. trade data due at 1330 GMT. Analysts said the numbers would be under closer scrutiny after the widening Japanese trade surplus with the United States announced earlier in the week week.

And the markets were also looking for some lead from U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, who was due to speak in Washington at 1500 GMT against a background of figures on Wedneday showing U.S. consumer prices rose more than expected last month.
The Federal Reserve's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meets next week to decide whether to boost interest rates in a pre-emptive strike against inflationary pressures.
Interest rate concerns and the 19 point fall in the Dow overnight spooked bourses in Europe.
London, the continent's biggest exchange, was down almost three quarters of a percent by 1000 GMT, Paris was down 1.5 percent and Frankfurt had fallen over one percent.

London dealers said the market was likely to remain nervous in the wake of the strong U.S. data, which revived concerns not only about U.S. rates but also that British rates would rise soon after the May 1 general election.
"Interest rates ought to go up now and whoever wins the election is going to have to put them up," the head of equity sales said. "The only question is how much they will have to be raised by."
A little of the heat was taken out of the worries by British data early Thursday showing inflation fell to 2.7 percent in February, from 2.8 in January.
Rob Hayward of Bank America said: "The figures are pretty much in line. I think people were still a little bit nervous after yesterday and there may be a sigh of relief in the markets now."
In Frankfurt German shares were dragged lower by the impact of a falling equity futures market combined with the weak sentiment emerging from the United States.
Dealers blamed lower U.S. Treasuries and the fall in the Dow overnight for the weakness. "All in all, there is a lot of pressure on the market today," one said.
The main market focus was the restarting of trade in Thyssen and Krupp-Hoesch after two days of suspension related to Krupp's attempt to produce a merger of their steel businesses.
In Paris it was a similar story and the blue chip CAC-40 index took a steep slide. Traders said profit-takling was partly to blame as Thursday was the last day of the month's trading account.
They said the markets were similarly cautious over possible U.S. interest rate tightening and sharp falls in bond markets.
CURRENCIES AT 1000 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.6750 marks and 122.72 yen, compared with Wednesday's late European levels of 1.6808 and 122.59.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1000 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 29.5 points at 4,302.6.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 38.56 at 3,277.37.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 37.93 points at 2,558.55.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold opened at $352.35 in Zurich versus London's close of $348.95 on Wednesday. Silver was at $5.24.
